messages.content: You shoulder the door open against the wind and stamp the snow off your boots on the mat. Blood is dripping from your hand onto the floorboards. "Sorry about the mess. My car's in the ditch half a mile down. Is anyone here?"

The lobby of the Kessler Pass Lodge is a long room of dark pine, lit by a fire that has burned down to red coals and a row of brass lamps along the reception desk. Antlers over the hearth, a rack of old wooden skis by the door, a smell of woodsmoke and wet wool. The wind keeps leaning on the windows as if it means to come in after you.

A woman in her forties comes through a door behind the desk, drying her hands on a dish towel. She has dark hair cut short, reading glasses pushed up on her head, and the steady look of someone who has handled worse than a bleeding stranger at nine at night. She sees your hand and drops the towel on the counter.

"Here. Sit." She pulls a chair out from the wall by the fire. "I'm Ilse, I run the night desk. Don't drip on the rug, it's older than me." She is already reaching under the desk for a first-aid box. "Is it just the hand, or did you hit your head too? People who go in the ditch on this road usually hit something."

You sit and hold your right hand up, palm open. A gash runs across it below the fingers. "Just the hand. The side mirror snapped off when I slid, and I grabbed it like an idiot. I didn't hit my head."

Ilse kneels in front of you and turns your right hand toward the lamp. The cut runs across the palm, clean but deep, and it opens when you flex your fingers. She presses a wad of gauze into it and folds your fingers over it.

"Hold that. Hard." She stands and goes to the foot of the staircase. "Odile! Are you still awake? I've got one for you."

A door opens upstairs and a small white-haired woman in a cardigan comes down, one hand on the banister, a leather bag in the other as though she had been expecting the call. "I am seventy-three years old, Ilse, I am always awake." She sits on the hearth stones in front of you and peels back the gauze with quick, unbothered fingers. "Dr. Ferrand. Retired, but my hands are not. This wants stitches, three I think. I have lidocaine, if you are not one of those people who faint."
You glance at the needle, then look away at the fire. "Go ahead. I won't faint. Thank you, Doctor."

Odile works quickly. The lidocaine stings and then the palm goes numb and distant, as though it belongs to someone else. She puts in three neat stitches across your right palm, ties them off, and wraps the hand in a white bandage that leaves your fingers free.

"Three," she says, snipping the thread. "Keep it dry. No gripping anything for a week, and that includes steering wheels and mirrors." She notices your left wrist as she packs her bag: a heavy steel watch on a worn leather strap, its hands stopped. "Your watch has died, I think. It says ten past four."

Ilse brings a mug of tea and sets it on the hearth beside you. "On the house, for bleeding on my floor. When you can hold a pen, I'll need you to sign in. We've rooms, God knows. Nobody comes up the pass in January if they can help it."

You turn your wrist to look at the watch. "It stopped years ago. It was my father's, Leo. My mother had 'for L.' engraved on the back the year they married. I just wear it." You stand and go to the desk with your tea. "I'll sign in now. Tess Morrow. Just the one night, hopefully."

Odile pauses on the stairs with her bag. "Then it is not broken, it is keeping somebody's time," she says. "Ten past four. Good night, Ms. Morrow." She nods to both of you and goes up to bed, and a door closes softly on the floor above.

Ilse opens a leather-bound register on the counter and turns it to face you. "Morrow. Tess." She writes the name herself, to spare your bandaged hand, then takes a key with a heavy brass tag from the board behind her. "Fourteen. Second floor, at the end of the corridor, past the ice machine that doesn't work. It's the warmest room in the house because it's over the kitchen. Breakfast from seven, if the cook makes it up the hill, which he won't." She pauses. "Do you have bags in that car? Because I'm not sending anybody down the road for them tonight."

You lift the leather satchel hanging from your shoulder. "This is all I need tonight. The rest can wait." You keep a hand on the satchel strap. "Is there a phone? My cell has had no signal since the second switchback."

"There's a landline in the office, and a payphone in the hall that hasn't taken coins since 1998." Ilse lifts the hinged flap of the counter. "Office is through here. Dial nine for outside. It works when the wind lets it."

The office is a narrow room crowded with filing cabinets, a space heater ticking under the desk, and a corkboard covered with road reports and a laminated avalanche map of the pass. The phone is an old beige thing with a curly cord. When you lift the receiver there is a dial tone, faint and scratchy, as though the line runs a very long way through snow.

Ilse stays in the doorway with her arms folded, not hovering, but not leaving either. "If you need the tow service, it's Halvorsen's in town, and they won't come before the plough does. If it's anything else," she adds, "the walls in this place are thick and I don't listen at doors."
You dial a number from memory and wait. After a while you hang up. "Voicemail." You turn to Ilse. "Who else is staying here tonight?"

Ilse counts on her fingers. "Odile, who you've met. She's here every winter, writing a book she won't let anyone read. A Swedish couple, the Lindqvists, Pia and Anders, honeymoon, God help them, in January. Bernard, who owns the place, asleep in the back since eight. Remy, our kitchen boy, sixteen, who'll be eating cereal in the pantry at midnight. And me." She shrugs. "That's the Kessler Pass Lodge in winter. Six people and a lot of empty rooms."

She switches off the office light and walks you back to the foot of the stairs. Outside, the wind has picked up into a long, low howl, and somewhere above the roofline something creaks and settles. "That's just the snow on the roof," she says. "You get used to it. Or you don't, and you leave in the morning." She hands you the brass key to room fourteen. "Anything else before I lock the front door?"

You glance at the dark stairs, then lean on the counter and lower your voice. "One thing. I'd rather not keep something in my room tonight. Is there anywhere down here that nobody would think to look?"

Ilse takes her reading glasses off her head, folds them, and puts them in her shirt pocket, which seems to be how she gives something her full attention. She looks at the satchel, then at you.

"There's a safe in the office," she says. "Everybody who has ever worked here knows the combination, including two cooks I fired, so I wouldn't call it a hiding place." She glances along the counter: the register, the brass bell, a jar of wrapped mints, a rack of trail maps, and at the far end an old snow globe the size of a grapefruit, a little lodge and three fir trees under the glass, sitting on a heavy wooden base. "What size of something are we talking about?"

You take a small black USB key out of the inside pocket of the satchel and close your hand around it so only she can see it. "About this size. It's evidence for a claim I'm working on, a warehouse fire down in the valley. There are people who'd like it to disappear."

Ilse looks at the key for a long moment and does not ask the obvious questions, which you notice. Then she reaches down the counter and picks up the snow globe in both hands. The snow inside lifts and swirls around the little lodge.

"My grandmother's," she says. "Bernard thinks it's tacky and wants it gone, which is why it stays." She turns it upside down. The wooden base is a separate piece, felt underneath, and when she twists it, it unscrews with a dry little squeak. Inside is a hollow where a music box used to be; the mechanism is long gone, leaving a space about the size of a matchbox. "It played 'Edelweiss' until I was twelve. Nobody has opened this thing in thirty years except me."

You drop the USB key into the hollow in the base of the snow globe. You screw the base back on yourself, as tight as your bandaged hand allows, and set the globe back at the end of the counter where it was. "Then that's where it lives. Ilse, nobody else can know. Not Bernard, not the doctor, nobody. Please."

Ilse watches you put the snow globe back exactly where it stood, then reaches over and turns it a quarter turn so the little lodge faces the door again, the way it always does. "If it faces the wrong way, Bernard notices," she says. "He notices nothing else in this building, but he notices that."

She puts her glasses back on her head. "Nobody will hear it from me. I've worked nights in hotels for twenty years, Ms. Morrow. You'd be amazed at the things people leave with the night desk, and I have never once told anyone where anything was." She lifts the counter flap and lets it down behind her with a soft thump. "If someone comes asking, I'll tell them the truth: the safe's in the office and everybody knows the combination."
You let out a breath and some of the stiffness goes out of your shoulders. "Thank you. Really. I'll get out of your way." You start for the stairs, then turn back. "What time do you go off shift?"

"Seven, when Bernard shuffles out with his coffee and pretends he's been up for hours." Ilse is already turning down the brass lamps one by one along the counter, so that the lobby sinks into firelight. "If you need anything in the night, ring zero on the room phone. It rings in the office and I'll hear it unless I'm in the kitchen stealing Remy's cereal."

The stairs creak under you all the way up. The second-floor corridor is long and narrow, with a strip of red carpet worn pale down the middle, framed photographs of skiers from the 1950s, and at the far end the dead ice machine Ilse mentioned, humming faintly although it does nothing. The door of fourteen sticks, then gives. Inside it is warm, as promised: a brass bed with a thick quilt, a radiator clanking under the window, and beyond the glass nothing at all but snow driving sideways through the light from the porch below.
You lock the door, check the window latch, and sit on the edge of the bed. You try your cell phone once more, holding it up near the window.

One bar flickers in the corner of the screen, vanishes, flickers again. For three or four seconds you have signal, enough for the phone to buzz once in your hand with a message that must have been waiting since the valley. Then the bar is gone and stays gone.

The message is from an unknown number, sent at 6:42 that evening, four words long: "They know you have it." There is no name and no second message.

Below the window, at the edge of the porch light, the snow has already filled in your footprints from the road. The wind has dropped for the moment, and in the sudden quiet you can hear the old building ticking and settling around you, and from somewhere below, faint and tinny, Ilse's radio playing in the office.
You wake to grey light and a deep, total silence. You dress, check the corridor, and go down to the lobby.

The lobby is full of a flat white light from the windows, which are blank with snow to halfway up the glass. The fire has been built up again and a long table by the hearth has been laid for breakfast: a coffee urn, a basket of bread, a block of butter, jars of jam with handwritten labels.

Behind the desk, instead of Ilse, there is a heavy man in his sixties in a cardigan with leather elbow patches, holding a cup of coffee in both hands and staring at the telephone as if it had insulted him. He looks up when you come down. "You'll be fourteen. Morrow." He doesn't offer a hand. "Bernard Aucoin. It's my hotel, for what that's worth this morning." He sets the cup down. "The road's gone. Slid at about five, between the second and third switchbacks. I heard it from my bed, like a train. And the phone's dead since six." He picks up the receiver and holds it out to you, as if you might not believe him. There is no tone at all.
You take the receiver, listen, and hand it back. "How long does it usually take them to clear a slide like that?"

"Usually?" Bernard puts the receiver down with care. "Two days if it's small and they've got a machine free. A week if it's big and they don't. Last time it was nine days, in '09, and we ate a lot of soup." He jerks his chin toward the dining room. "The plough driver's in there. He came up last night behind you and got as far as the lot before the blade iced up. He's been on his radio since dawn, he'll know more than me."

Through the double doors to the dining room you can see a young man in a hi-vis jacket hunched over a table with a handheld radio, a map of the pass spread out under his elbows. Across the room, at a table by the window, a fair-haired couple in matching sweaters are eating toast very slowly, the way people eat when they have nowhere to be and are starting to realise it.

Bernard pours a second cup of coffee and pushes it across the counter toward you without asking. "Ilse said you came in bleeding. She said nothing else, which with Ilse means there's a story."

You take the coffee with your left hand and nod your thanks. "No story. I hit a mirror." You go through to the dining room and stop at the plough driver's table. "Bernard says you've got a radio. Any news from down the mountain?"

The young man looks up. He is maybe twenty-five, with a shaved head, a short beard and the red, raw hands of someone who works outside all winter. "Dev," he says. "Dev Raman. County roads." He taps the map with a pencil. "Slide came down right here, across both lanes, maybe four metres deep at the middle and two hundred long. Dispatch says they can't send the big blower till the weather breaks, and the weather's not breaking before Thursday. So." He spreads his hands. "Welcome to the Kessler Pass Lodge, everybody. Checkout's Friday at the earliest."

The radio on the table crackles and a woman's voice says something about the lower road and a jackknifed truck. Dev turns it down. "Radio's only good to dispatch and only when the wind's right. Phone lines run along the road, so they're under the slide too." He looks at your bandaged hand, then at your face. "You the one whose car's in the ditch below the bend? Blue hatchback? I passed it last night. Your back window was open. I figured you knew."
You set your coffee down. "Open? I closed every window before I walked up. Was anyone near the car?"

Dev frowns and scratches his beard. "Didn't see anybody. It was blowing pretty hard, I wasn't looking at much except the road. But it was open, the back one on the driver's side, and there was snow on the seat." He shrugs. "Could've popped when you went in the ditch. Glass does funny things in the cold."

At the window table the fair-haired woman has stopped eating and is watching you openly, with the frank curiosity of someone who has run out of other entertainment. She is in her early thirties, with a long plait over one shoulder. Her husband, a tall man with wire-rimmed glasses, puts a hand on her arm as if to say don't, and she ignores it.

"Sorry," she calls across the room, not sounding sorry. "Pia Lindqvist. We couldn't help hearing. Somebody broke into your car? Up here?" Her English is perfect, with a faint lilt. "That's the most exciting thing that's happened since we arrived, and we've been here four days."

You give the couple a polite smile. "Probably just the cold, like Dev says. Nothing in there worth stealing." You sit at an empty table with your coffee and some bread, where you can see the front door.

Pia looks faintly disappointed and goes back to her toast. Her husband gives you a small apologetic nod across the room, the kind of nod that says he has been married to her for exactly long enough to know she will try again later.

For a while nothing happens. Remy, a gangly boy in a stained apron, comes out of the kitchen with a tray of scrambled eggs and sets it on the buffet without a word, then retreats. Odile comes down with a notebook under her arm, takes a plate, and sits by the fire, writing in tiny handwriting. Dev's radio mutters. The snow keeps falling past the windows, slow and heavy now that the wind has dropped.

Then, at a quarter to ten, someone knocks on the front door. Not a guest's knock: three hard blows of a fist. Bernard looks up from the desk. Through the frosted glass panel of the door you can see the shape of a tall figure, and behind him nothing but white.
You stay in your seat and watch the door, your hand resting on the satchel at your side.

Bernard opens the door and a gust of snow comes in with the man. He is tall, in his fifties, in a black wool coat that was not made for mountains, and leather city shoes soaked dark to the ankle. Snow is caked in his short grey hair. He stamps his feet on the mat, as you did last night, and takes off a pair of thin leather gloves finger by finger.

"Thank God," he says to Bernard, in a pleasant, educated voice. "My car's off the road two miles down, on the other side of what I'm told is an avalanche. I climbed over the top of it. Not an experience I'd recommend." He laughs, and the sound is easy and practised. "Gabriel Stroud. I need a room, a phone and a very large drink, not necessarily in that order."

Bernard tells him about the phone. Stroud listens, nods, takes it well. While Bernard opens the register, Stroud's eyes go round the lobby the way a man's eyes go round a room he means to remember: the stairs, the office door, the board of keys, the desk, the dining room. They pass over you at your table, and stop, and stay a moment longer than they need to.
You finish your coffee without hurrying, then take your plate back to the buffet, close enough to the desk to hear what name Stroud signs.

Stroud signs with a fountain pen he takes from his own inside pocket, a fat black thing with a gold clip, and his signature is large and looping. Bernard gives him eleven, on the second floor, three doors down from yours. "Lunch is at one, if the boy cooks," Bernard says. "Bar opens when I say so."

"Then I'll be your best customer." Stroud caps the pen, and as he turns from the desk he finds you standing at the buffet and smiles as though you were old friends. "You're the other casualty of the road, I think. I saw a little blue car on the way up, nose in a snowbank. I hope that wasn't yours."

Up close he smells of cold air and expensive cologne. His eyes are pale grey and very steady, and they rest on your bandaged hand, then on the satchel, then come back to your face. He holds out his hand. "Gabriel. We'll be neighbours for a while, it seems. Better to be friends than strangers in a snowed-in hotel, don't you think? I've read the novels. The strangers always come off worse."
You shake his hand briefly with your left hand. "Tess. That was my car. What brings you up the pass in January, Gabriel?"

"Business, I'm afraid. Always business." He lets go of your hand and spreads his own in a gesture of mock apology. "I'm a lawyer, which I know is nobody's favourite thing to be stuck in a lodge with. I represent a company down in the valley, a storage firm, Kessler Valley Cold Storage, who had a very bad week before Christmas." He watches your face as he says it, pleasantly, without any change of expression. "A fire. Perhaps you saw it on the news. Total loss. My client is desperate to have the insurance settled so they can rebuild and keep their people employed."

He takes a cup and fills it from the urn. "I was driving up to meet a former employee of theirs who's supposed to be staying in the village on the far side of the pass. A bookkeeper. She left rather suddenly and took some files with her that don't belong to her." He blows on his coffee. "Small world, these mountains. Everybody seems to be going somewhere with something that belongs to somebody else."

Across the dining room, Pia Lindqvist has given up all pretence of not listening.
You give him a level look. "Small world," you agree. "I hope you find your bookkeeper." You pick up your satchel and go upstairs to your room.

The corridor is empty and quiet, lit by the grey snow light from a window at the far end. The ice machine hums. Your door is closed, the way you left it, and the key turns in the lock the way it should.

Inside, the room is not the way you left it. It is tidy, almost: someone has been careful. But the quilt is smoother than you left it and tucked in at the foot, which you did not do. The drawer of the bedside table is closed all the way, and you left it open a crack because it sticks. Your spare sweater, folded on the chair, is folded the other way, sleeves outward. In the bathroom, the lid of the toilet cistern is sitting very slightly askew.

Nothing seems to be missing. Whoever it was had perhaps twenty minutes, while you were at breakfast, and was looking for something small.
You check the window latch, then go back down to the desk. "Bernard. Who has keys to the rooms besides the guests?"

Bernard looks up from a ledger of what appear to be grocery orders. "Me. Ilse. The master key's on my belt and the spare's in the office safe." He touches a ring of keys clipped to his trousers. "Why?"

When you tell him, his heavy face goes still and then red. "Nobody on my staff goes into a guest's room without knocking. Remy does the rooms on Tuesdays, and it's not Tuesday." He lowers his voice and glances toward the stairs. "And the safe, well. Half the valley knows that combination. I keep meaning to change it." He rubs his face with both hands. "Is anything missing? Do I need to... I don't know what I'd do. Lock everybody in the bar until the plough comes?"

Behind you, the office door opens and Dev comes out with his radio, catching the end of it. He looks from Bernard to you. "Someone go in your room? Same day as your car window?" He whistles softly. "That's not the cold, then."
You keep your voice low. "Nothing's missing. I'd rather this stays between the three of us for now. Dev, who was in the lobby while I was at breakfast?"

Dev thinks about it, counting off on his raw fingers. "Me, in the office, on the radio, most of the time. Bernard at the desk, mostly." Bernard nods. "The Swedes went up and came back down, I think, she'd forgotten her book. The doctor went up and down once for a pen. The kid was in the kitchen." He frowns. "And the lawyer guy, when he came in, Bernard gave him the key and he went up to drop his coat before he came back down to talk to you. Five minutes, maybe less."

"And I went to the cellar for wood," Bernard says slowly. "Ten minutes. Maybe fifteen. The desk was empty." He looks at the board behind him, where the keys hang on their brass hooks, then at the stairs. "Anybody could have gone up."

The front door rattles in a gust. Upstairs, a door closes. Bernard looks at you with a mixture of worry and stubborn pride. "This is my house," he says. "Tell me what you need me to do."
You think it over. "Nothing yet. Just keep an eye on who goes upstairs, and don't mention this to anyone. When does Ilse come on?"

"Seven tonight." Bernard looks relieved to be asked something he can answer. "She sleeps in the staff cottage behind the kitchen when the road's shut, so she's here, just asleep. I wouldn't wake her unless the building's on fire. Last person who woke Ilse before noon is still apologising."

Dev tucks the radio into his jacket. "I'll be around. Not going anywhere, am I?" He gives you a crooked smile and wanders back into the dining room, where he sits down two tables from Stroud, who has returned and is reading a paperback from the lodge's shelf with every sign of contentment.

The afternoon stretches ahead of you, white and slow. Snow slides off the roof every so often with a soft roar and a thump. In the dining room, Stroud turns a page, glances up over the top of his book toward the lobby where you are standing, and goes back to reading.
You spend the afternoon by the fire with a book you don't read, keeping the stairs and the desk in view. When it starts to get dark, you go to the window to look at the snow.

Outside, the light is going blue. The snow has stopped falling and lies over everything in deep, smooth drifts that bury the porch rail and round off the shapes of the cars in the lot into soft white hills. Dev's plough sits at the edge of the lot like a sleeping animal, its blade furred with ice. Beyond it, the road simply ends in white. There is no sound at all.

Behind you the lodge is filling with its evening noises: Remy banging pots in the kitchen, the clink of Bernard setting out glasses in the bar, Pia laughing at something her husband said. Stroud has moved to a leather armchair near the bar, a glass of whisky on the table at his elbow, and is talking quietly with Anders Lindqvist about skiing in the Alps.

Then every light in the building goes out at once. The hum of the refrigerators stops. In the sudden dark there is only the red glow of the fire, and Pia's voice saying, "Oh!" and from somewhere upstairs, Odile calling, perfectly calm, "Bernard, the power."
You stay where you are, your back to the window, and let your eyes adjust to the firelight. You count the shapes you can see in the room.

In the firelight the lobby turns to shadows and orange edges. You can make out Pia and Anders together by the bar, Pia's pale plait, Anders's glasses catching the glow. Remy appears in the kitchen doorway with a lit candle, his face young and alarmed above it. Bernard is coming around the end of the desk with a big rubber flashlight, swearing under his breath in French.

The leather armchair by the bar is empty. The whisky glass is still on the table beside it.

"Generator," Bernard announces to the room. The flashlight beam swings across the ceiling. "It's in the cellar. It starts, eventually, if you talk to it nicely. Remy, candles in the dining room, the box under the sink. Dev!" he calls toward the dining room. "I need a strong arm on the pull cord." There is no answer from the dining room. The beam swings that way and finds an empty table, a radio, a map. "Dev?"

name: snowline
system:
You are the narrator and game master of an interactive story, "Snowline".

The player controls the protagonist, an insurance claims investigator. You control the world and every other character.

Rules:
- Narrate in second person, present tense ("you"), in prose. Put spoken words in double quotes.
- Never decide the protagonist's actions, words, thoughts or feelings. Describe the world and the other characters, then leave room for the player to act.
- Characters only know what they have seen, heard or been told inside the story. Keep track of who knows what.
- Keep each reply between one and three paragraphs.
- If the player writes out of character, for example "Pause scenario", "Stop the roleplay", or a message in parentheses starting with OOC, stop narrating at once and answer plainly as an assistant, outside the story.

Setting: the present day, early January. The Kessler Pass Lodge is an old timber hotel at the top of a mountain pass, two hours from the nearest town. The protagonist has driven up from the valley, where she is investigating a suspicious warehouse fire for the insurer, and carries evidence that someone would pay to recover.
